one_liner: Single-file C interpreter for LLVM bitcode and early WebAssembly; about 96x faster than LLVM's lli interpreter on one SHA-1 run.
what_it_does: VMIR loads a .bc (LLVM bitcode built for the le32-unknown-nacl target) or a .wasm module and runs it inside a host C program, with a small built-in libc. The embedding API in src/vmir.h is a C interface: vmir_create() over a caller-supplied memory block (split into register-frame, stack and heap areas), vmir_load(), vmir_run() to call main(), and vmir_find_function()/vmir_vm_function_call() to call guest functions, plus hooks for an external-function resolver and filesystem operations. It is not a drop-in for lli or any wasm runtime API; it is meant for shipping C/C++ plugins as bitcode or wasm.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of walking LLVM IR like lli's interpreter, VMIR lowers each function at load time: it leaves SSA, runs liveness analysis with an interference-matrix register allocator and move coalescing, then applies peephole fusions (GEP+load/store into lea addressing, compare+branch, compare+select, multiply+add, load+cast) and emits a compact 16-bit-word instruction stream with type- and constant-specialised opcodes (for example ADD_R32C). The stream is executed with computed-goto threaded dispatch over register frames, and on 32-bit ARM Linux an optional JIT emits native code for the instruction classes it supports. Guest loads and stores in release builds are plain host-pointer arithmetic with no bounds check, which also removes per-access cost.
when_to_use: You must execute LLVM bitcode from C without linking LLVM, and lli's interpreter is the alternative (the README's only baseline).
Small embedded or plugin hosts that want one C file (src/vmir.c includes the rest) and a fixed, caller-allocated memory arena.
32-bit ARM Linux targets where the built-in JIT applies (README: Raspberry Pi 2 SHA-1 run 17.5 s with JIT vs 1m42s interpreted).
Plain C plugins compiled with an old clang that use only the subset of libc VMIR implements and no vector types.
Research or teaching on lowering SSA IR to a register-based threaded interpreter.
when_not_to_use: Running untrusted code: release builds do no guest bounds checks (only the VM_TRACE debug build checks), so guest pointers and libc calls such as fread can touch host memory outside the arena, and guest division by zero reaches the host as a native fault.

Modern toolchains: open issue #14 (2018) reports bitcode from Ubuntu Bionic's clang fails to parse ('Type (i8) (index:0) is not a pointer'), issue #5 says clang 3.9 does not work, and LLVM's later opaque-pointer bitcode is not handled by any commit after 2018-08-29.

Modern WebAssembly: the parser rejects resizable memories and tables, imported memories, tables and globals, multi-value returns, and accepts only constants in init expressions (Go-built wasm fails, issue #9); for wasm use wasm3, WAMR or Wasmi.
C++ programs needing the STL, code relying on SIMD/vector types, or programs needing a full libc.
Performance-critical x86-64 work: the interpreter is about 12x slower than native on the README's x86 run and there is no x86 JIT.

integration.dependencies: none (libm; TLSF allocator vendored in tlsf/ and enabled by the Makefile with -DVMIR_USE_TLSF)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 with GNU extensions (-std=gnu99; computed goto and case ranges); issue #7 reports it only builds with clang, not gcc (not re-tested here). Guest code needs a 2016-2017 era clang emitting le32-unknown-nacl bitcode.
integration.platforms: Interpreter: any POSIX host the code builds on (Makefile targets x86-64 host, armv7 and ppc64 with big-endian byte swapping). JIT: 32-bit ARM Linux/Android only.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; state lives in the per-instance ir_unit_t, but no statement about concurrent instances or calls

gotchas: No sandboxing in release builds: CHECK_MEM_ACCESS() in src/vmir_mem.c is empty unless VM_TRACE is defined, HOSTADDR(ea) is hostmem + a 32-bit guest address, and libc shims like vmir_fread pass guest buffers and lengths straight to host fread without a length check.

Seven memory-safety reports against the wasm/bitcode loader were filed on 2024-03-06 (issues #18-#24: null derefs, heap-buffer-overflow in wasm_call, wild reads and writes, stack overflow) and are unanswered, so loading untrusted files can crash or corrupt the host.
Guest code must be compiled with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize and multi-file programs must be llvm-link'ed into one .bc; the le32-unknown-nacl target is required.

The benchmark's lli baseline is LLVM's IR interpreter, which the README itself calls not intended to be fast; lli's JIT mode, the LLVM version and the bitcode optimisation level (the test Makefile builds -O0, -O1 and -O2) are not stated, so the 96x figure says little about VMIR against any production engine.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick VMIR over wasm3, WAMR or Wasmi only when your input is LLVM bitcode rather than wasm and you can live with an unmaintained, unsandboxed interpreter; for any WebAssembly workload those siblings are maintained, spec-conformant, bounds-checked and have published cross-runtime numbers that VMIR lacks.
verified_claims_summary: The README's single table times test/misc/src/sha1test.c hashing 64 MB of random data: on an unspecified Core i7 at 3.2 GHz, VMIR 4.8 s versus LLVM lli 7 min 39 s (about 96x, derived from page data) and native 0.39 s (VMIR about 12x slower); on a Raspberry Pi 2, VMIR 1m42s, VMIR JIT 17.5 s, native 3.54 s. No compiler or LLVM versions, flags for native or lli, or the bitcode optimisation level are given, and the README does not say whether the times include bitcode loading and lowering (main.c's -s option times only vmir_run).
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-08-29 with 18 open issues including unanswered 2024 memory-safety reports; MIT-licensed and easy to vendor as one C file, but only usable with old clang bitcode and only safe for trusted code.
